README.html.title: Deodesy | Deodesy
README.html.summary: Deodesy Deodesy is C#/.NET version of Chris Veness's amazing work Geodesy Functions. Geodesy Functions is written in JavaScript and contains dozens of functions to make calculations about: Geodesic calculations (distances, bearings, etc) covering both spherical earth and ellipsoidal earth models, and both trigonometry-based and vector-based approaches. Ellipsoidal-earth coordinate systems covering both historical datums and modern terrestrial reference frames (TRFs). Mapping functions including UTM/MGRS and UK OS Grid References.

docs/api/Deodesy.Library.LatLonSpherical.summary: Class LatLonSpherical Namespace Deodesy.Library Assembly Deodesy.Library.dll Provides functions for spherical geodesy, based on the Haversine formula and other spherical geometry calculations. These functions are adapted from Chris Veness's original JavaScript geodesy library. public class LatLonSpherical Inheritance object LatLonSpherical Inherited Members object.Equals(object) object.Equals(object, object) object.GetHashCode() object.GetType() object.MemberwiseClone() object.ReferenceEquals(object, object) object.ToString() Methods AlongTrackDistanceTo(Coordinate, Coordinate, Coordinate) Calculates the along-track distance from a start point to the point on a great-circle path that is closest to a current point. public double AlongTrackDistanceTo(Coordinate currentPoint, Coordinate startPoint, Coordinate endPoint) Parameters currentPoint Coordinate The current coordinate. startPoint Coordinate The starting coordinate of the great-circle path. endPoint Coordinate The ending coordinate of the great-circle path. Returns double The along-track distance in kilometers. Examples var start = new Coordinate(53.2611, -0.7972); // N of Lincoln var end = new Coordinate(48.5734, 7.7161); // Strasbourg var current = new Coordinate(53.1887, 0.1334); // E of Lincoln var geo = new LatLonSpherical(); double alongTrackDist = geo.AlongTrackDistanceTo(current, start, end); Console.WriteLine($"Along-track distance: {alongTrackDist:F2} km"); // Output: Along-track distance: 53.7 km Remarks This is the distance from the start point to where a perpendicular from the current point crosses the great-circle path. Exceptions ArgumentNullException Thrown if currentPoint, startPoint, or endPoint is null. Bearing(Coordinate, Coordinate) Calculates the initial bearing (direction) from a start point to an end point. public double Bearing(Coordinate startPoint, Coordinate endPoint) Parameters startPoint Coordinate The starting coordinate. endPoint Coordinate The ending coordinate. Returns double The initial bearing in degrees, in the range 0 to 360. Examples var p1 = new Coordinate(51.51, 0.0); // London var p2 = new Coordinate(38.89, -77.03); // Washington D.C. var geo = new LatLonSpherical(); double bearing = geo.Bearing(p1, p2); Console.WriteLine($"Initial Bearing: {bearing:F2}°"); // Output: Initial Bearing: 324.26° Exceptions ArgumentNullException Thrown if startPoint or endPoint is null. CrossTrackDistance(Coordinate, Coordinate, Coordinate) Calculates the cross-track distance from a current point to a great-circle path defined by two other points. public double CrossTrackDistance(Coordinate currentPoint, Coordinate startPoint, Coordinate endPoint) Parameters currentPoint Coordinate The current coordinate. startPoint Coordinate The starting coordinate of the great-circle path. endPoint Coordinate The ending coordinate of the great-circle path. Returns double The cross-track distance in kilometers. Examples var start = new Coordinate(53.2611, -0.7972); // N of Lincoln var end = new Coordinate(48.5734, 7.7161); // Strasbourg var current = new Coordinate(53.1887, 0.1334); // E of Lincoln var geo = new LatLonSpherical(); double crossTrackDist = geo.CrossTrackDistance(current, start, end); Console.WriteLine($"Cross-track distance: {crossTrackDist:F2} km"); // Output: Cross-track distance: -31.93 km Remarks The cross-track distance is the shortest distance from the current point to the great-circle path. Exceptions ArgumentNullException Thrown if currentPoint, startPoint, or endPoint is null. CrossingParallels(Coordinate, Coordinate, double) Calculates the pair of meridians at which a great circle defined by two points crosses a given latitude. public double[]? CrossingParallels(Coordinate startPoint, Coordinate endPoint, double latitude) Parameters startPoint Coordinate The starting coordinate of the great circle. endPoint Coordinate The ending coordinate of the great circle. latitude double The latitude (in degrees) for which to find the crossing meridians. Returns double[] An array of two doubles representing the longitudes (in degrees, wrapped to -180 to 180) of the crossing points, or null if the great circle does not reach the given latitude. Examples var p1 = new Coordinate(0, 0); // Equator, Prime Meridian var p2 = new Coordinate(30, 90); // 30°N, 90°E var geo = new LatLonSpherical(); double[]? crossingLons = geo.CrossingParallels(p1, p2, 15); // Find where it crosses 15°N if (crossingLons != null) { Console.WriteLine($"Crossing Longitudes at 15°N: {crossingLons[0]:F2}°, {crossingLons[1]:F2}°"); // Output: Crossing Longitudes at 15°N: 27.65°, 152.35° } else { Console.WriteLine("Great circle does not cross 15°N."); } Exceptions ArgumentNullException Thrown if startPoint or endPoint is null. Destination(Coordinate, double, double) Calculates the destination point and final bearing when traveling along a great circle arc for a given start point, initial bearing, and distance. public Coordinate Destination(Coordinate startPoint, double distance, double bearing) Parameters startPoint Coordinate The starting coordinate. distance double The distance to travel in kilometers. bearing double The initial bearing in degrees. Returns Coordinate A Coordinate object representing the destination point. Examples var p1 = new Coordinate(51.51, 0.0); // London var geo = new LatLonSpherical(); var destPoint = geo.destination(p1, 7794.0, 300.0); // Travel 7794 km on bearing 300° Console.WriteLine($"Destination: Lat {destPoint.Latitude:F2}, Lon {destPoint.Longitude:F2}"); // Output: Destination: Lat 34.01, Lon -100.83 Exceptions ArgumentNullException Thrown if startPoint is null. Distance(Coordinate, Coordinate) Calculates the distance (in kilometers) between two points on the Earth's surface using the Haversine formula. public double Distance(Coordinate startPoint, Coordinate endPoint) Parameters startPoint Coordinate The starting coordinate. endPoint Coordinate The ending coordinate. Returns double The distance in kilometers. Examples var p1 = new Coordinate(51.51, 0.0); // London var p2 = new Coordinate(38.89, -77.03); // Washington D.C. var geo = new LatLonSpherical(); double distance = geo.Distance(p1, p2); Console.WriteLine($"Distance: {distance:F2} km"); // Output: Distance: 5908.38 km (approx) Exceptions ArgumentNullException Thrown if startPoint or endPoint is null. DistanceInNm(Coordinate, Coordinate) Calculates the distance (in nautical miles) between two points on the Earth's surface using the Haversine formula. public double DistanceInNm(Coordinate startPoint, Coordinate endPoint) Parameters startPoint Coordinate The starting coordinate. endPoint Coordinate The ending coordinate. Returns double The distance in nautical miles. Examples var p1 = new Coordinate(51.51, 0.0); // London var p2 = new Coordinate(38.89, -77.03); // Washington D.C. var geo = new LatLonSpherical(); double distanceNm = geo.DistanceInNm(p1, p2); Console.WriteLine($"Distance: {distanceNm:F2} nm"); // Output: Distance: 3190.27 nm Exceptions ArgumentNullException Thrown if startPoint or endPoint is null. FinalBearing(Coordinate, Coordinate) Calculates the final bearing (direction) when arriving at an end point from a start point. public double FinalBearing(Coordinate startPoint, Coordinate endPoint) Parameters startPoint Coordinate The starting coordinate. endPoint Coordinate The ending coordinate. Returns double The final bearing in degrees, in the range 0 to 360. Examples var p1 = new Coordinate(51.51, 0.0); // London var p2 = new Coordinate(38.89, -77.03); // Washington D.C. var geo = new LatLonSpherical(); double finalBearing = geo.FinalBearing(p1, p2); Console.WriteLine($"Final Bearing: {finalBearing:F2}°"); // Output: Final Bearing: 229.31° Remarks The final bearing will differ from the initial bearing by varying degrees according to distance and latitude. Exceptions ArgumentNullException Thrown if startPoint or endPoint is null. Intermediate(Coordinate, Coordinate, double) Calculates the point at a given fraction along the great-circle path between two points. public Coordinate Intermediate(Coordinate startPoint, Coordinate endPoint, double fraction) Parameters startPoint Coordinate The starting coordinate. endPoint Coordinate The ending coordinate. fraction double The fraction along the path (0.0 for startPoint, 1.0 for endPoint, 0.5 for midpoint). Returns Coordinate A Coordinate object representing the intermediate point. Examples var p1 = new Coordinate(51.51, 0.0); // London var p2 = new Coordinate(38.89, -77.03); // Washington D.C. var geo = new LatLonSpherical(); var intermediatePoint = geo.Intermediate(p1, p2, 0.25); // 25% of the way Console.WriteLine($"Intermediate Point (25%): Lat {intermediatePoint.Latitude:F2}, Lon {intermediatePoint.Longitude:F2}"); // Output: Intermediate Point (25%): Lat 53.82, Lon -21.65 Exceptions ArgumentNullException Thrown if startPoint or endPoint is null. Intersection(Coordinate, double, Coordinate, double) Calculates the point of intersection of two great-circle paths. public Coordinate? Intersection(Coordinate firstPoint, double firstBearing, Coordinate secondPoint, double secondBearing) Parameters firstPoint Coordinate The starting point of the first path. firstBearing double The initial bearing of the first path in degrees. secondPoint Coordinate The starting point of the second path. secondBearing double The initial bearing of the second path in degrees. Returns Coordinate A Coordinate object representing the intersection point, or null if no intersection or paths are coincident. Examples var p1 = new Coordinate(51.8853, 0.235); // Cambridge var brng1 = 108.549; // Bearing from Cambridge var p2 = new Coordinate(49.0034, 2.5735); // Paris var brng2 = 32.435; // Bearing from Paris var geo = new LatLonSpherical(); var intersection = geo.Intersection(p1, brng1, p2, brng2); if (intersection != null) { Console.WriteLine($"Intersection: Lat {intersection.Latitude:F2}, Lon {intersection.Longitude:F2}"); // Output: Intersection: Lat 50.99, Lon 4.50 (near Brussels) } else { Console.WriteLine("No intersection found."); } Exceptions ArgumentNullException Thrown if firstPoint or secondPoint is null. MaxLatitude(Coordinate, double) Calculates the maximum latitude reached when traveling on a great circle from a start point with a given initial bearing (using Clairaut’s formula). public double MaxLatitude(Coordinate startPoint, double bearing) Parameters startPoint Coordinate The starting coordinate. bearing double The initial bearing in degrees. Returns double The maximum latitude in degrees. Examples var p1 = new Coordinate(51.51, 0.0); // London var geo = new LatLonSpherical(); double maxLat = geo.MaxLatitude(p1, 90.0); // Bearing East Console.WriteLine($"Max Latitude: {maxLat:F2}°"); // Output: Max Latitude: 51.51° Remarks The maximum latitude is independent of longitude; it will be the same for all points on a given latitude. Negate the result for the minimum latitude (in the Southern Hemisphere). Exceptions ArgumentNullException Thrown if startPoint is null. MidPoint(Coordinate, Coordinate) Calculates the midpoint between two points on the Earth's surface. public Coordinate MidPoint(Coordinate startPoint, Coordinate endPoint) Parameters startPoint Coordinate The starting coordinate. endPoint Coordinate The ending coordinate. Returns Coordinate A Coordinate object representing the midpoint. Examples var p1 = new Coordinate(51.51, 0.0); // London var p2 = new Coordinate(38.89, -77.03); // Washington D.C. var geo = new LatLonSpherical(); var midpoint = geo.MidPoint(p1, p2); Console.WriteLine($"Midpoint: Lat {midpoint.Latitude:F2}, Lon {midpoint.Longitude:F2}"); // Output: Midpoint: Lat 52.04, Lon -43.58 Exceptions ArgumentNullException Thrown if startPoint or endPoint is null.

docs/md/getting-started.html.summary: Getting Started Welcome to Deodesy, a robust .NET library for geographical calculations. This guide will help you set up the library and start performing geodesic computations in your applications. Prerequisites Before you begin, ensure you have the following installed: .NET SDK (6.0 or later recommended) A C# IDE (Visual Studio, JetBrains Rider, or VS Code) Building from Source To build the library locally, clone the repository and use the .NET CLI: # Navigate to the library directory cd src/Deodesy.Library # Build the project dotnet build -c Release The compiled binaries will be available in the src/Deodesy.Library/bin/Release/netstandard2.0 directory. Target Framework & Compatibility Deodesy targets .NET Standard 2.0, providing maximum reach across the .NET ecosystem. Platform Minimum Version .NET & .NET Core 2.0+ .NET Framework 4.6.1+ Mono 5.4+ Xamarin.iOS / Xamarin.Android 10.14+ / 8.0+ Installation You can integrate Deodesy into your project by adding a reference to the project file or the compiled DLL. Via .NET CLI Run the following command from your project's directory: dotnet add reference path/to/Deodesy.Library.csproj Via Visual Studio Right-click your project in Solution Explorer. Select Add > Project Reference... Browse and select Deodesy.Library.csproj. Quick Start Example Here is a simple example demonstrating how to calculate the distance between two geographical points using the spherical model. using Deodesy.Library; // Define coordinates for London and Washington D.C. var london = new Coordinate(51.5074, -0.1278); var washington = new Coordinate(38.8951, -77.0364); // Initialize the spherical geodesy utility var geodesy = new LatLonSpherical(); // Calculate distance in kilometers double distance = geodesy.Distance(london, washington); Console.WriteLine($"Distance between London and DC: {distance:F2} km"); // Output: Distance between London and DC: 5908.38 km (approx) Next Steps Explore the API Reference for advanced features.

docs/md/introduction.html.title: Introduction to Deodesy | Deodesy
docs/md/introduction.html.summary: Introduction to Deodesy Deodesy is designed to provide .NET developers with a reliable and efficient solution for geographical calculations. Originating as a C#/.NET port of Chris Veness's highly respected JavaScript Geodesy Functions, Deodesy aims to maintain the accuracy and breadth of the original library while integrating seamlessly into the .NET environment. Why Deodesy? Geographical calculations are fundamental to many applications, from mapping and navigation to logistics and environmental science. Deodesy addresses the need for a robust, well-tested, and comprehensive geodesy library in C#. By porting a widely-used and validated JavaScript library, Deodesy offers: Proven Accuracy: Leveraging the algorithms and extensive testing of the original Geodesy Functions. C#/.NET Integration: Native C# implementation, allowing for easy integration into .NET projects without interoperability overhead. Comprehensive Features: A rich set of functions covering various aspects of geodesic computations. Maintainability: Written with modern C# practices, ensuring readability and ease of maintenance. Core Concepts Deodesy operates on fundamental geodesic principles. Key concepts you'll encounter include: Coordinates: Representing points on the Earth's surface using latitude and longitude. Distances: Calculating the shortest path between two points (great-circle distance). Bearings: Determining the direction from one point to another. Ellipsoidal vs. Spherical Models: Understanding the differences between modeling the Earth as a perfect sphere versus a more accurate ellipsoid. Further Reading Getting Started API Reference Original JavaScript Geodesy Functions by Chris Veness

index.html.title: Welcome to Deodesy | Deodesy
index.html.summary: Welcome to Deodesy Deodesy is a powerful and comprehensive C#/.NET library for performing geodesic calculations. The name Deodesy is a portmanteau of .NET and Geodesy, reflecting its mission to bring robust and accurate geographical computations to the .NET ecosystem. It is a faithful port of Chris Veness's renowned JavaScript Geodesy Functions, maintaining high precision while providing a first-class developer experience for .NET users. What is Geodesy? Geodesy is the scientific discipline that deals with the measurement and representation of the Earth. It involves understanding the Earth's gravitational field, its geodynamic phenomena (polar motion, Earth tides, crustal motion), and its three-dimensional time-varying distribution of mass. Features Deodesy provides a wide range of functionalities, including: Geodesic Calculations: Perform precise calculations for distances, bearings, and other parameters across both spherical and ellipsoidal Earth models. This includes both trigonometry-based and vector-based approaches for maximum flexibility and accuracy. Ellipsoidal Earth Models: Support for various ellipsoidal-earth coordinate systems, encompassing both historical datums and modern terrestrial reference frames (TRFs). Mapping Functions: Tools for working with popular mapping systems such as UTM/MGRS (Universal Transverse Mercator / Military Grid Reference System) and UK OS Grid References. Getting Started To begin using Deodesy, please refer to our Getting Started guide. API Reference For detailed information on all available classes and methods, consult the API Documentation.
